extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, employers, educators, and the educated public interested in technical education and monetary policy (late 19th-century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: An advocacy/analytic essay arguing what kinds of education, institutions, and social supports are appropriate for working-class handicraftsmen (and how exceptional talent among them should be identified and fostered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid delaying entrance into practical life
rubrics_metrics.description: The two things to be avoided are the delay of the entrance of boys into practical life, and the substitution of exhausted bookworms for shrewd, handy men in our works and factories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping boys at school beyond thirteen or fourteen is neither practicable nor desirable for those intended to be handicraftsmen; excessive book-learning can be a direct disqualification for practical trades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-education of handicraftsmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-education of handicraftsmen is a real danger: encouraging the notion that brain-work is intrinsically nobler than handiwork can be 'a deadly mischief' to the workman and to industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education must be calibrated to serve practical employability and not merely produce examination success or social prestige; otherwise it may lead to replacement of practical men with 'exhausted bookworms'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good foreman
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity, probity, knowledge of men, ready mother-wit, supplemented by a good knowledge of the general principles involved in his business, are the making of a good foreman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical virtues and situational intelligence are more important for a foreman than extensive formal learning; excessive schooling may impair the habit of mind required for the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce elementary science and art in elementary schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction in elementary science and in art should be more thoroughly incorporated in the educational system rather than administered 'by driblets'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current provision is piecemeal; better integration at elementary level is urged, though only rudiments can be introduced without displacing other important branches of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accessible practical evening classes (Science and Art Department)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evening classes bring instruction to the doors of factories and workshops, are responsive to popular demand, and can develop indefinitely as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These classes should be practical, accessible after working hours, and are effective means for workers to acquire scientific and artistic knowledge; the department should continue to promote practical instruction and teacher development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress 'pot-teaching' (teaching to the exam) and train teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'teaching for the pot' — instruction aimed at producing examination passes rather than genuine knowledge — and improve teacher quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers need instruction not only in subject matter but in the purposes for which they teach; institutions should provide facilities for teachers to learn their business thoroughly and aid in suppression of exam-focused teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow supplementary training after work-life begins
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary training in science, art, and foreign languages should be available after the workman's life has begun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because elementary schools can only offer rudiments, continuing education via evening classes, apprenticeships, or other means is necessary for skill development compatible with working lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a ladder and machinery to identify and promote talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential foundation needed is machinery for winnowing out capacities and giving them scope — a 'ladder, reaching from the gutter to the university' so every child can climb as far as he is fit to go.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify exceptional abilities in elementary or evening classes, secure relevant apprenticeships, enable teacher careers, and make the highest training accessible to those of genius; investment in such persons yields large social and economic returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove artificial obstacles and provide social support for advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every working-lad should feel society has done what lies in its power to remove needless and artificial obstacles from his path, and that if he has capacity and industry a hand is held out to help him along.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social organization should create transparent pathways (except natural limits) so capable workers can reach appropriate social positions; this is the essential foundation for promoting education among handicraftsmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage private and civic institutional support (livery companies, Society of Arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful societies (e.g., the livery companies, Society of Arts) should organize and subsidize instruction in technology for persons employed in factories and workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Society of Arts (since 1872) organized technology instruction and received subsidies; such institutions can form committees and take steps with lasting influence on teaching of handicrafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coins are certified bullion; purchasing power determined by pure metal content
rubrics_metrics.description: Coins are simply stamped bullion; the purchasing power of money is regulated by the quantity of pure metal in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stamp or design does not materially increase purchasing power except for a tiny convenience premium; coin should be treated as a commodity certified by seal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of fixity of standards (weight and measures) for commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce and science depend upon absolute adherence to certain standards of weight and upon the assumption of the invariability of laws like gravitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fixity of standards (e.g., definition of a pound sterling or avoirdupois) is imperative even if philosophically difficult; otherwise exchange and measurement become unstable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debasement of coinage (state or private) is economically harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal and legislative attempts to make a part equal to the whole (debasement) have caused great evils; laws forcing debased coin to circulate at face value are used to enforce the swindle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cases (Rome, France, China, England) show debasement leads to disorder, famine, suffering; debasement accompanied by tyrannical laws distorts commerce and harms subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin-clipping as private degradation of coinage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coin-clipping reduces the value of coins without public authority and differs from state debasement; it is less mischievous because no one is compelled to accept clipped coins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clipping was historically widespread despite severe penalties; it creates transactional disputes and market disorder but forces losses only on those who accept clipped pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuing fresh honest coin may not displace bad money due to Gresham's-law dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing plentiful new, honest milled coins does not necessarily displace bad money because 'bad money drives out good'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical attempts to flood markets with good coin led to the new coins vanishing from circulation; policymakers must account for the incentives that cause people to hoard good coin and spend bad coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject policy of intentionally depreciating new coinage to match bad money
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to depreciate the standard of new coin to the level of trash in circulation (e.g., making a shilling worth ninepence) are misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument illustrated by William Lowndes' recommendation and its critics: legally authorizing payment with less metallic value effectively authorizes a de facto tax/transfer and is dishonest and economically harmful.
